newsitem.title: USA: Miami, Fla., audit delayed, bond questions remain.
newsitem.headline: Miami, Fla., audit delayed, bond questions remain.

text.p: Miami's external auditor still has not completed its review of the city's fiscal 1996 finances, in part because of questions about whether the city violated any bond regulations.

KPMG Peat Marwick LLP had been expected to finish its audit by the end of March for the year that ended September 30, 1996. But the leader of the firm's Miami audit team, Jose Rodriguez, told a state-appointed oversight board Monday that the firm was still awaiting several pieces of missing data needed to finish Miami's audit.
Among them, he said, was a report from the city's independent bond counsel "as to whether they were in violation of any laws."

The city hired the New York firm of Hawkins Delafield & Wood in January to work with a local firm, Holtzman, Krinzman, Equels & Furia, to determine whether Miami met disclosure requirements after its financial situation deteriorated and to examine its general handling of bond proceeds.
Attorney Sonny Holtzman told Reuters during a break in the meeting Monday that, "We're still fact collecting. We're not ready to give an opinion."
City Manager Ed Marquez told the board that, "Our gut tells us that we shouldn't have any bond problems."

However, board members again raised questions about the $72 million special obligation pension bond issue sold in December 1995. Proceeds were to be used to make pension fund contributions for 1995, 1996 and part of 1997.
City officials previously acknowledged that some of the bond proceeds were "borrowed" to help meet operating expenses in fiscal 1996.

Oversight board member Cynthia Curry said Monday that the city's fiscal 1996 operating expenses exceeded revenues by $18.75 million, and that restricted cash, including some bond proceeds, were used to cover the gap.
"Bond funds were used for other than the purpose they were received for," Curry told the board.
"It is questionable," Curry told Reuters later.

But Marquez said bond money had not been misspent, and that the confusion stemmed from the fact that the city pooled its restricted and unrestricted cash, and because bond proceeds were to be used for pension contributions, which are an operating expense.
The city has since segregated its accounts and put debt service revenues into an escrow account overseen by a trustee.
"Now that they have been segregated, we shouldn't have that problem," Curry said.

Rodriguez said he was also waiting to hear from regulators whether there was any pending action that could affect Miami's finances, before he could sign off on the audit. The Securities and Exchange Commission has declined to comment, but city officials previously said the agency was probing Miami bond deals.
Marquez said the final audit was expected on May 5 and that "The numbers we have today are materially going to stay the same."
The audit is expected to confirm that the city's cumulative deficit was $68 million at the beginning of 1997.
The board has approved a 1997 budget that closed the gap, largely through land sales and other one-time revenues.
The city has until April 15 to submit a balanced five-year budget to the oversight board, which then has another month to review it and seek revisions.

"It may go back one or twice. I don't want to prejudge it," said Lt. Gov. Buddy MacKay, who heads the oversight panel. "I want to have a clear way of understanding that recurring revenues are going to cover recurring expenses.

City officials also disclosed Monday that Miami was still several months behind in reconciling its bank statements. The trust account is current but the payroll and workers compensation account is only reconciled through December, the deposit accounts through November and accounts payable through October.
Marquez said a new computer program had been installed and temporary workers added to bring the accounts up to date.
